# Motion

- Route: `/tools/motion`
- Kind: `tool`
- Category: `motion`
- Slug: `motion`

## Summary

Draw or import an SVG, animate it on a keyframe timeline, and export animated SVG, Lottie, React, JavaScript, Flutter or GIF, all in your browser. (SVG animation)

## Details

Motion is an SVG editor with an animation timeline, built into Media Manipulator. Open an SVG file (or a Lottie animation) and every shape becomes a layer you can select, move, recolour and animate, or start from a blank canvas and draw with the rectangle, ellipse, line, pen and text tools. Each animated property gets its own track of keyframes, with easing presets, a curve editor for custom easing, and hold keys for instant jumps. One-click animators add stroke draw-on, motion along a path, shape morphing, gradient colour changes, mask animation and blur. When it moves the way you want, export it as an animated SVG, a Lottie file, a React component, a JavaScript or TypeScript module, a Flutter widget or a GIF. Editing and every export run in your browser, so your artwork is never uploaded to export it; the server is only asked to count the export against your daily allowance.
### What it does
- Imports SVG files into an editable layer tree (groups, paths, shapes, text, images, gradients, masks and clip paths) and imports Lottie JSON animations with their keyframes, each file up to 4 MB.
- Draws new artwork with rectangle, ellipse, line, pen (Bézier) and text tools, and edits path nodes directly on the canvas.
- Animates position, scale, rotation, skew, opacity, fill, stroke and stroke width on a keyframe timeline with linear, ease-in, ease-out, ease-in-out, custom cubic-bezier and hold easing.
- Adds six one-click animators: stroke draw-on, motion along a path with optional auto-rotate, shape morphing, gradient stop colours, mask and clip-path animation, and blur.
- Exports a static SVG (always free and never counted), an animated SVG that plays without any library, Lottie JSON, a React component, a JavaScript or TypeScript module, a Flutter widget and an animated GIF, all generated on your machine.
### How to use it
1. Open or draw: Import an SVG or Lottie file, or draw shapes and paths on a blank canvas.
2. Animate: Move the playhead and change a property: the timeline records a keyframe for it.
3. Shape the timing: Pick an easing preset, draw a custom curve, add holds, or apply a one-click animator.
4. Export: Choose a format; the server counts one export, then your browser builds and downloads the file.
### Supported formats
- Input: SVG, Lottie JSON, Motion project (.json)
- Output: Static SVG, Animated SVG, Lottie JSON, React (.tsx), JavaScript / TypeScript, Flutter (.dart), GIF
- Editing, preview and every export run in your browser. Only a count of each export is sent to our servers.
### Technical details
- The animated SVG export uses pure CSS keyframes whenever every effect can be expressed in CSS in Chrome, Firefox and Safari. Shape morphs, moving gradient stops and blur need a script, so those files embed a trimmed copy of anime.js (MIT licence, about 31 KB of script, roughly 13 KB after gzip) with its licence notice at the top.
- Shape morphing normalises both shapes to the same number of curve segments and lines up their start points and winding, so the morph does not twist. Two shapes that cannot be matched hold instead of morphing.
- The Lottie writer targets the Lottie 1.0.1 specification and the LottieFiles "Basic" feature set. Anything Lottie cannot carry (such as filters, text or advanced masks) is listed after the download; nothing is dropped silently. The reader uses the same list in the other direction.
- GIF export renders frames one at a time, transfers each to a Worker, and encodes with an encoder written for Media Manipulator: one global palette sampled from five frames spread across the span, dithering off by default (flat vector art has few colours and dither adds noise), a frame delay of round(100 / fps) centiseconds, and transparency kept only when the canvas background is transparent. Output is capped at 2 GB and the dialog shows a size estimate before you start.
- Imported SVGs are cleaned on the way in: scripts, event handlers, external references and other unsafe content are removed, and the editor rebuilds unsupported markup from an allow-list instead of inserting it as HTML. Markup it cannot model is kept as an opaque layer that round-trips unchanged.
- The export counter is a single database transaction: the format lock and the caps are checked, then the counter and an export row are written together. A refused export writes nothing and costs nothing; an export the browser then cancels or fails has already been counted.
### When not to use it
Motion animates vector artwork; it does not edit video or photographs. If your starting point is footage, Darkroom is the editor and the video-to-GIF page turns a clip into a GIF. It is also not a vectoriser for complex raster images: a photograph traced to paths will be heavy and the result will not animate meaningfully. Animations that depend on filters, text effects or advanced masks will not survive a Lottie export intact (the dialog lists what was dropped), so for those targets keep to the animated SVG, React or JavaScript exports. And MP4 or WebM output depends on your browser's WebCodecs support and on your plan, so check the plan table before planning a video deliverable.
### Use cases
- Logo and icon animation: Draw a logo on with a stroke animation, or make an icon bounce, spin or change colour on hover.
- Loaders and UI micro-animations: Build spinners and progress animations and export them as CSS-only SVG or a React component.
- Lottie for mobile apps: Export Lottie JSON for the iOS, Android, web and Flutter Lottie players, or edit an existing Lottie file.
- Animated illustrations: Move parts of an illustration along paths, morph shapes into each other and export a GIF for chat or email.
### FAQ
Q: Is Motion free?
A: Yes. Opening Motion, drawing, animating, saving in this browser and exporting a static SVG are free, unlimited and need no account. Daily limits and file caps depend on the plan; quote them only from the live plan block. The plan table on this page shows each plan's live allowance and formats.
Q: Which formats can I export?
A: Static SVG, animated SVG (CSS, or a small inline script when needed), Lottie JSON, a React component (.tsx), a JavaScript or TypeScript module, a Flutter widget (.dart) and an animated GIF. By default animated SVG is on every plan, Lottie from the free account up, and React, JS/TS, Flutter and GIF from Premium up. Which of these your plan includes, and the daily number of exports, are shown in the plan table on this page.
Q: What are the limits?
A: Animated exports are counted per day and reset at midnight UTC; a refused export is not counted, but an export you cancel after the count has been taken is. Daily limits and file caps depend on the plan; quote them only from the live plan block. SVG and Lottie imports are capped at 4 MB each, GIF export at 50 fps and 2 GB of output. Every current number is in the plan table on this page and on the pricing page.
Q: Can I animate an SVG I already have?
A: Yes. Import any SVG and its groups, paths, shapes, text, gradients, masks and clip paths become editable layers. Parts the editor cannot edit, such as patterns or complex filters, are kept and exported unchanged, and anything unsafe (scripts, event handlers or external links) is removed and listed after the import.
Q: Does it support Lottie?
A: Yes, in both directions. You can import a Lottie JSON file to edit it (the import counts as one unit on the free plan and up), and export your animation as Lottie JSON for lottie-web and the iOS, Android and Flutter Lottie players. Features one side cannot represent are listed in the dialog instead of being dropped silently.
Q: Which browsers support video export?
A: GIF export works in all modern browsers. MP4 and WebM export rely on WebCodecs, the browser's built-in video encoder, which is available in Chrome and Edge and in recent versions of Safari and Firefox depending on the codec; the export dialog checks your browser and says when it cannot encode. The plan table on this page shows which plan includes each video format.
Q: What licence applies to the exported code?
A: Your animation belongs to you. When an animated SVG or a code export needs a runtime, it uses anime.js, which is MIT-licensed; its copyright notice is written at the top of the file and must be kept there. Flutter exports use the flutter_svg (MIT) or webview_flutter (BSD-3-Clause) package. Everything else in the file is generated from your project. The open-source libraries the editor uses are listed on our licences page.
Q: Where are my projects stored?
A: Without an account, projects are kept only in this browser, so clearing your browser data removes them. When you are signed in you can save a project to your account; it then syncs between devices, autosaves while you work, follows the retention period you chose and can be deleted from your Account page.

## Routing

When to send a visitor here: Send visitors here when they want to animate an SVG or Lottie file, draw simple vector shapes and animate them on a keyframe timeline, or export animation as animated SVG, Lottie, React, JavaScript, Flutter or GIF. Phrasings like "animate my logo", "make a Lottie animation" or "edit an SVG animation" fit.
When to send them elsewhere: If the starting point is video footage, use Darkroom (content-studio) for editing or Convert Video to Animated GIF (convert-video-to-animated-gif) for a GIF. To turn a raster logo into vector paths first, use Convert PNG to SVG (convert-png-to-svg); it is not meant for photographs.
Related tools: content-studio (edit video footage on a timeline); convert-video-to-animated-gif (make a GIF from a video clip); convert-png-to-svg (trace simple raster art into SVG before animating); convert-svg-to-png (export a still raster of the artwork)
